title: Mastering the Power of the Pause - Coach Heather Fundamentals Part 1
author: Coach Heather
summary: Kicking off a four-part 'Coach Heather Fundamentals' series, this piece makes the case that pausing before reacting is a trainable leadership skill rather than hesitation or avoidance. Coach Heather argues that modern work culture is structurally built for immediate reaction, and that leaders who cannot create space between stimulus and response end up turning minor stressors into larger problems through impulsive emails, decisions, or arguments. Her concrete tool is a 90-second pause: noticing emotional activation, stepping away and breathing, then consciously choosing a response rather than defaulting to the first reactive impulse. The piece frames this small habit as the foundation for more intentional, effective communication and decision-making under pressure.
points: Coach Heather reframes pausing as an active leadership skill rather than avoidance or hesitation, arguing the space it creates between stimulus and response is 'our place of personal empowerment.'
Her concrete tool is a 90-second pause protocol: notice activation, breathe, step away if possible, then consciously choose a response rather than defaulting to reaction.

She names four things leaders don't have to do reflexively: respond to every email immediately, solve every problem in the moment, believe the first story their fear tells them, or participate in everything designed to keep them on high alert.

The piece diagnoses modern work culture itself as structurally built for urgency and immediate reaction, making deliberate pausing a countercultural leadership discipline rather than a soft-skill nicety.
quotes: The ability to pause creates space between what happens and what we do next.

Pausing gives us an opportunity to move out of automatic reaction and back into more intentional thinking. It can help us communicate more effectively, make better decisions, and avoid turning a moment of stress into a much bigger problem.
There will always be pressure, difficult conversations, unexpected challenges, and moments when emotions run high. We cannot control all of that.
My hope is that you begin to see pausing not as avoidance or hesitation, but as a leadership skill.
The next time you notice yourself becoming emotionally activated, don't immediately send the email, answer the question, make the decision, or continue the argument.
And you do not have to participate in everything around you that is designed to keep you in a constant state of high alert. You can pause.
